beats.narration_text: Hear how every word is still ringing when the next one arrives? David Byrne, the singer from Talking Heads, wrote a book about this, called How Music Works. His big idea is that a room doesn't just hold music. It shapes it.

props.heading: A room shapes the music in it
props.sentence: Every room you play in is asking you a question.
props.caption: David Byrne, How Music Works: music is made to fit the place it will be heard.
props.source: Simulated echo: our own impulse response (T30 4.7 s, measured). Not a measured room. · David Byrne, How Music Works (2012), ch. 1 “Creation in Reverse”

beats.narration_text: The way I'd put it: the room asks a question, and the player answers.

props.heading: How a room shapes music
props.source: David Byrne, How Music Works (2012), ch. 1 “Creation in Reverse” · the research in this video

beats.narration_text: In two thousand fifteen, two researchers in Berlin measured how much one player changes from room to room. The cellist Jean-Guihen Queyras played all six of Bach's cello suites in seven European concert halls. They measured how much each hall echoed, and how fast he played. In the most echoing halls, he slowed down. Musicians have advised that since at least seventeen fifty-two: give the echo time to clear.

props.heading: One cellist, seven halls
props.xLabel: how much echo the hall has
props.schematicNote: Shape only. The paper reports a fitted curve, not these points.
props.caption: Most echoing halls → he played slower, as Quantz advised in 1752.
props.source: Schärer Kalkandjiev & Weinzierl (2015), Proc. Third Vienna Talk on Music Acoustics, pp. 215–219 · Psychomusicology 25(3) · Quantz (1752), as cited there

beats.narration_text: But in the driest halls, the ones with almost no echo, he slowed down too. Too much echo, slower. Too little echo, also slower. One measure of the hall's echo accounted for about seventy-four percent of how his tempo moved.

props.heading: He slowed down at both ends
props.xLabel: how much echo the hall has
props.schematicNote: Shape only. The paper reports a fitted curve, not these points.
props.caption: Driest halls → also slower. One cellist, seven halls.
props.source: Schärer Kalkandjiev & Weinzierl (2015), Proc. Third Vienna Talk on Music Acoustics, pp. 215–219 · Psychomusicology 25(3)

beats.narration_text: Why both? In echoing halls, he told them, he lets the pauses run longer. In dry halls, the researchers think a player holds notes longer, to fill in for an echo that isn't there. Same answer. Opposite questions.

props.heading: Same answer, opposite questions
props.asks: too much echo, or too little
evidence: Echoing hall (his words): let the pauses run longer
Dry hall (the researchers' explanation): hold notes longer
props.source: Schärer Kalkandjiev & Weinzierl (2015), Proc. Third Vienna Talk on Music Acoustics, pp. 215–219 · Psychomusicology 25(3), interviews and discussion

beats.narration_text: Try it yourself first. In a moment, clap once. If the clap hangs in the air, your room has echo. If it dies right away, it's dry. Go ahead.

props.heading: First: clap once, and listen.
props.asks: clap once: does it hang, or die?
evidence: Strong answer: names what the room did (blurred your words, or swallowed them)
props.source: Our listening heuristic, not a measurement

beats.narration_text: Now say the sentence, every room you play in is asking you a question, at the pace your room seems to want.

props.heading: Now: say the sentence at your room's pace.
props.asks: clap once: does it hang, or die?
evidence: Strong answer: names what the room did (blurred your words, or swallowed them)
props.source: Our listening heuristic, not a measurement
